items.definition: Traditional harvesting of moliço from the Ria, the economic activity for which the moliceiro boat was originally designed.
Flat bottom of the hull, allowing the boat to sail in the shallow waters of the Ria.
Low sides of the hull, making it easier to bring the moliço-gathering rakes and their catch into the boat.
Rakes used to gather moliço from the Ria bed and haul it into the boat.
Two kinds of pine, the woods used to build the moliceiro, chosen as part of its distinctive construction.
Simple handcrafted wooden rod acting as the master builders' ruler for building the whole boat; only experienced builders can interpret it.
Decorated panels on the boat, each pairing a drawing with a caption that must be read together to convey a message.
Bow, the front of the boat, where two of the decorated panels are placed.
Stern, the rear of the boat, where the other two decorated panels are placed.
Maintenance or fitting-out work on moliceiro boats, carried out throughout the year whenever owners request it.
Master boatbuilder who builds moliceiros and passes the craft knowledge on to apprentices.
Master painter who decorates the moliceiro panels.
Traditional naval carpentry craft that gives the moliceiro its distinctive structure, set apart from other boats of the Ria.
Flat bottom and shallow draught allowing navigation in shallow lagoon waters without running aground.
To run aground in shallow water, a risk the boat's hull shape is designed to avoid.
Pine wood, native and abundant locally, used for building because it performs well in humid environments.
Stone pine, used for the ribs (cavernas) and the braços of the boat.
Maritime pine, used for all parts of the boat other than the ribs and braços.
Overall length of the moliceiro hull.
Maximum beam (width) of the boat.
Depth of the hull, measured as its height at the side.
Cargo-carrying capacity of the boat, essential for gathering moliço.
The complete set of ribs of the hull, divided between stern and bow.
Ribs of the hull, on which the bottom planks are fixed.
Bottom planks fixed over the ribs, of variable width.
Covered, lockable bow compartment that served as sleeping quarters for crews gathering moliço.
Curved piece ending the highest point of the bow; the stern's highest point is also called bica.
Two opposed wooden pieces below the bica, used to tie the towline and rest rakes and poles at moorings.
Towline tied to the golfiões of the bow.
Poles rested on the golfiões at the mooring.
A fitting on the bow, named but not described in this part.
A fitting on the bow, named but not described in this part.
The highest point of the stern.
Small closed compartment inside the stern where salt, fish or salted meat was stored for the crew.
Removable lid in front of the cagarete, serving as the helmsman's seat and the place for the water barrel.
The skipper or helmsman who controls the boat.
Movable platform over the ribs at the helmsman's feet.

Part passing through the head (cabeça) of the rudder.
Transverse timber in the hull with a hole through which the mast passes.
The round hole in the traste through which the mast is passed.
Fore-and-aft piece set low in the hull between two frames, with a square hole receiving the mast foot.
Thick pine or eucalyptus pole that holds the yard from which the sail hangs; it passes through the enora and sits in the coicia.
Upper end of the mast, with a rectangular slot running port to starboard for the halyard.
Rectangular slot in the masthead acting as a sheave through which the ostaga runs.
Rope that runs through the slot at the top of the mast.
Yard carried by the mast, from which the sail hangs.
Broad white trapezoidal sail that moves the boat; formerly decorated for river pilgrimages, now with flags on festive days.
Rear side of the trapezoidal sail.
Lower side of the sail.
Front side of the sail.
Upper side of the sail, tied to the yard.
Trapezoidal pine boards lowered into the water that create a force against leeway; combined with sail thrust they drive the boat forward.
Rope passing through two holes in the toste head that ties it to the mast.
Windward side; one toste is raised on this side.
Leeward side; the other toste is half-immersed on this side to resist drifting.
Sideways drift of the boat, which the toste's anti-drift component cancels.
Wooden boards fixed along both sides from bow to stern to raise the sides and prevent flooding.
Small final board closing the side up to the bow, after the two main falcas.
Propulsion by pushing a pole against the lagoon bed, used in calm or near quays; deck is treated for grip.
Pitch and sawdust applied to the bow deck and sides to give grip and stop slipping while poling.
Towing the boat by a rope from the bank, used occasionally in narrow channels or against tide or wind.
The usual method of propulsion, sailing under the sail.
Rope attached to the sail and to the bow block, used to tension the sail so the boat gains ground to windward.
Pulley at the bow spout used to control sail tension when sailing close to the wind.
Sailing close to the wind to gain windward distance.
Small rope at the sail's lower part adjusting the exposed surface and so regulating the boat's speed.
Leeward drift of the boat, resisted by the half-immersed toste.
